notes.front: What is a separately stated item on an S corporation return?
notes.back: An item passed through to shareholders on its own line of Schedule K-1, such as a capital gain, rather than inside ordinary business income.
notes.explanation: The instructions give net short-term and long-term capital gains and other portfolio gains as items passed through separately.
notes.example: Like a shared bill that lists the wine per diner while the food is simply split as one total.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Line 17b. Investment Expenses”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: required to be passed through separately to the shareholders on Schedule K-1, such as net short-term capital gain or loss, net long-term capital gain or loss, and other portfolio gains or losses

notes.front: What is the accumulated adjustments account (AAA)?
notes.back: An S corporation account that generally reflects its accumulated undistributed net income for post-1982 years.
notes.explanation: An S corporation with accumulated earnings and profits must keep the AAA to work out the tax effect of its distributions.
notes.example: Like a running tally of profit already taxed to the owners but not yet paid out to them.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule M-2, Column (a). Accumulated Adjustments Account”, PDF p. 50
notes.evidence: The accumulated adjustments account (AAA) is an account of the S corporation that generally reflects the accumulated undistributed net income of the corporation for the corporation’s post-1982 years. S corporations with accumulated earnings and profits (AE&P) must maintain the AAA to determine the tax effect of distributions

notes.front: What is a shareholder’s stock basis in an S corporation?
notes.back: The shareholder’s basis in the shares, generally their cost, adjusted every year for the corporation’s income, losses, deductions and distributions.
notes.explanation: The shareholder, not the corporation, must keep the records; Schedule K-1 supplies the yearly figures.
notes.example: Like a savings balance: profits taxed to you add to it, and cash you take out or losses you use come off it.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: You are responsible for keeping the information needed to figure the basis of your stock in the corporation. Schedule K-1 provides information to help you figure your stock basis at the end of each corporate tax year. The basis of your stock (generally, its cost) is adjusted annually

notes.front: What is a shareholder’s debt basis (loan basis) in an S corporation?
notes.back: The basis of the shareholder’s own loans to the corporation: generally the balance the corporation owes them, after reductions and restorations.
notes.explanation: Losses and deductions left over once stock basis is used up reduce this loan basis next.
notes.example: Like a second bucket that catches losses once the stock bucket is empty.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis of loans”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The basis of your loans to the corporation is generally the balance the corporation owes you, adjusted for any reductions and restorations of loan basis (see the instructions for box 16, code E). Any amounts described in (3) and (4), earlier, not used to offset amounts in (1), earlier, or to reduce your stock basis

notes.front: Who is a 2% shareholder of an S corporation?
notes.back: Someone who directly or indirectly owns, on any day of the tax year, more than 2% of the stock or of the voting power.
notes.explanation: For fringe benefit purposes such a person is treated like a partner in a partnership, not like an employee.
notes.example: Like an owner who also draws a salary: for staff perks, the tax rules see the owner first and the employee second.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “Exception for S corporation shareholders”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: A 2% shareholder for this purpose is someone who directly or indirectly owns (for any day during the tax year) more than 2% of the corporation's stock or stock with more than 2% of the voting power. Treat a 2% shareholder as you would a partner in a partnership for fringe benefit purposes

notes.front: What is the built-in gains tax?
notes.back: A section 1374 tax on an S corporation’s net recognised built-in gain, where it was once a C corporation or holds former C corporation assets.
notes.explanation: Net unrealised built-in gain is measured at the start of the first S corporation year: asset value over adjusted basis.
notes.example: Like an exit charge on growth in value that built up while the business was still a C corporation.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule B, Item 8”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: The corporation is liable for section 1374 tax if (a) and (b) above apply and it has a net recognized built-in gain (defined in section 1374(d)(2)) for its tax year.

notes.front: At most, how many shareholders may an S corporation have?
notes.explanation: A married couple (and their estates) count as one, and all members of a family may be treated as one.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: It has no more than 100 shareholders. You can treat an individual and his or her spouse (and their estates) as one shareholder for this test. You can also treat all members of a family

notes.front: A corporation’s stock is held by 104 people: 96 unrelated individuals and 4 married couples. How many shareholders does it have for the 100-shareholder test?
notes.back: B: 100, so it passes.
notes.choices:
A) 104, so it cannot elect
B) 100, so it passes
C) 102, so it cannot elect
notes.choicesExplained: A counts each spouse separately. C counts only half the couples as one.
notes.explanation: 96 individuals + 4 couples counted once each = 100, which is not more than 100.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: You can treat an individual and his or her spouse (and their estates) as one shareholder for this test.

notes.front: An S corporation’s only shareholders may be individuals, estates, certain trusts and {{c1::exempt organisations described in section 401(a) or 501(c)(3)}}.
notes.explanation: The list is closed: any other kind of owner stops the corporation qualifying.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Its only shareholders are individuals, estates, exempt organizations described in section 401(a) or 501(c)(3), or certain trusts described in section 1361(c)(2)(A).

notes.front: Three would-be shareholders of a new corporation planning an S election: which one would stop it qualifying?
notes.back: A: the partnership.
notes.choices:
A) A partnership owned by two of the founders
B) The estate of a founder who died last year
C) An American citizen living in Ohio
notes.choicesExplained: C is an individual and B is an estate; both are on the list of permitted shareholders.
notes.explanation: Partnerships are not among the permitted shareholders: individuals, estates, certain trusts and certain exempt organisations.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Its only shareholders are individuals, estates, exempt organizations described in section 401(a) or 501(c)(3), or certain trusts described in section 1361(c)(2)(A).

notes.front: May a nonresident alien own shares in an S corporation?
notes.back: No, other than as a potential current beneficiary of an electing small business trust.
notes.explanation: Having no nonresident alien shareholders is one of the tests on the Form 2553 list.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: It has no nonresident alien shareholders (other than as potential current beneficiaries of an ESBT).

notes.front: When is a corporation generally treated as having only one class of stock?
notes.back: When all its outstanding shares confer identical rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds.
notes.explanation: Differences in voting rights are disregarded, so the test looks only at economic rights.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: It has only one class of stock (disregarding differences in voting rights). Generally, a corporation is treated as having only one class of stock if all outstanding shares of the corporation's stock confer identical rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds.

notes.front: A corporation has voting and nonvoting common shares. Both carry the same rights to distributions and to liquidation proceeds. Does it have more than one class of stock for the S election?
notes.back: C: no; voting differences are disregarded.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: voting differences create a second class
B) Yes, unless the nonvoting shares are held by family
C) No: voting differences are disregarded
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the rule that voting rights are disregarded. B invents a family condition the rule does not have.
notes.explanation: Identical distribution and liquidation rights mean one class, whatever the voting rights.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: It has only one class of stock (disregarding differences in voting rights).

notes.front: What are two kinds of domestic corporation that cannot be S corporations whatever their shareholders?
notes.back: An insurance company taxed under subchapter L, and a bank or thrift using the reserve method for bad debts.
notes.explanation: The Form 2553 instructions also list a domestic international sales corporation, or former one, as ineligible.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: It isn’t one of the following ineligible corporations. a. A bank or thrift institution that uses the reserve method of accounting for bad debts under section 585. b. An insurance company subject to tax under subchapter L of the Code.

notes.front: By when must Form 2553 be filed for the S election to take effect for a given tax year?
notes.back: No more than 2 months and 15 days after that tax year begins, or at any time during the preceding tax year.
notes.explanation: The 2-month period runs from the day the year begins to the day before the matching date two months later; 15 days are then added.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “When To Make the Election”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: No more than 2 months and 15 days after the beginning of the tax year the election is to take effect, or • At any time during the tax year preceding the tax year it is to take effect.

notes.front: A new calendar-year corporation begins its first tax year on 3 February 2025 and wants S status from day one. What is the last day to file Form 2553?
notes.back: C: 17 April 2025.
notes.choices:
A) 2 April 2025
B) 3 May 2025
C) 17 April 2025
notes.choicesExplained: A stops at the end of the 2-month period without the extra 15 days. B adds a full 3 months.
notes.explanation: The 2-month period runs 3 February to 2 April; 2 April + 15 days = 17 April.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “When To Make the Election”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: the 2-month period begins on the day of the month the tax year begins and ends with the close of the day before the numerically corresponding day of the second calendar month following that month.

notes.front: Who must consent to an S election, and how?
notes.back: Every shareholder, by signing and dating column K of Form 2553 or a separate consent statement.
notes.explanation: Consent by each shareholder is the last of the tests a corporation must meet to elect.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Column K. Shareholder’s Consent Statement”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Each shareholder consents by signing and dating either in column K or on a separate consent statement.

notes.front: A married couple in a community property state hold S corporation stock that is community property. The stock is in the husband’s name. Who must sign the consent?
notes.back: B: both spouses.
notes.choices:
A) The husband only
B) Both spouses
C) Neither: couples count as one shareholder
notes.choicesExplained: A looks only at the name on the certificate. C mixes up the 100-shareholder count with the consent rule.
notes.explanation: Where spouses have a community interest in the stock or its income, both must consent.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Column K. Shareholder’s Consent Statement”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: If an individual and his or her spouse have a community interest in the stock or in the income from it, both must consent.

notes.front: Under the late-election relief in the Form 2553 instructions, within what period after the intended effective date must the late Form 2553 be filed?
notes.back: Within 3 years and 75 days.
notes.explanation: Outside that window, relief is still possible if the corporation and all shareholders reported as an S corporation, 6 months have passed since its first return, and no IRS notice followed.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Relief for Late Elections”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Form 2553 will be filed within 3 years and 75 days of the date entered on line E of Form 2553

notes.front: Who is generally taxed on an S corporation’s income?
notes.back: The shareholders, though the corporation may still owe tax on certain income.
notes.explanation: The built-in gains tax and the excess net passive income tax are examples of tax the corporation itself can owe.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Purpose of Form”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: The income of an S corporation generally is taxed to the shareholders of the corporation rather than to the corporation itself. However, an S corporation may still owe tax on certain income.

notes.front: Is an S corporation shareholder taxed on their share of income the corporation did not distribute?
notes.back: Yes: the share is taxable whether or not distributed.
notes.explanation: Schedule K-1 reports the shareholder’s share of income, which they include on their own return.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Purpose of Schedule K-1”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: You may be liable for tax on your share of the corporation’s income, whether or not distributed.

notes.front: Lena owns 40% of an S corporation all year. Its 2025 ordinary business income is $150,000, and it distributes $20,000 to her. How much ordinary business income does she report?
notes.choicesExplained: B reports only the cash she received. C subtracts the distribution from her share.
notes.explanation: 40% × $150,000 = $60,000. The $20,000 distribution does not change her share of income.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Purpose of Schedule K-1”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: You may be liable for tax on your share of the corporation’s income, whether or not distributed.

notes.front: Is a shareholder’s share of S corporation income subject to self-employment tax?
notes.back: No: it isn’t self-employment income.
notes.explanation: Contrast a sole proprietor, whose business profit is self-employment income.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “General Instructions”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: Your share of S corporation income isn’t self-employment income and it isn’t subject to self-employment tax.

notes.front: An S corporation earns $90,000 from sales and $4,000 of interest on a savings account it holds as an investment. Where does it report the interest?
notes.back: A: on Schedule K.
notes.choices:
A) On Schedule K, as portfolio income
B) On page 1 of Form 1120-S with the sales
C) Nowhere: S corporations don’t report interest
notes.choicesExplained: B nets an item that must be passed through separately. C is wrong: all income passes through to shareholders.
notes.explanation: Portfolio income and its deductions go on Schedule K rather than page 1, so they stay separately stated.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Passive Activity Limitations”, PDF p. 11
notes.evidence: Report portfolio income and related deductions on Schedule K rather than on page 1 of Form 1120-S.

notes.front: On the first day of a corporation’s first tax year as an S corporation, its AAA balance is {{c1::zero}}.
notes.explanation: The account then builds up from income earned only in S corporation years.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule M-2, Column (a). Accumulated Adjustments Account”, PDF p. 50
notes.evidence: On the first day of the corporation’s first tax year as an S corporation, the balance of the AAA is zero.

notes.front: An S corporation starts 2025 with AAA of $30,000. For 2025 it has ordinary income of $50,000, tax-exempt interest of $2,000, nondeductible expenses of $1,000 (none tied to tax-exempt income) and cash distributions of $60,000. Year-end AAA?
notes.choicesExplained: B adds the tax-exempt interest, which does not go into AAA. A ignores the nondeductible expenses.
notes.explanation: Tax-exempt interest stays out of AAA, and expenses come off before distributions: $30,000 + $50,000 = $80,000; − $1,000 = $79,000; − $60,000 = $19,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule M-2, Column (a). Accumulated Adjustments Account”, PDF p. 50
notes.evidence: Generally, decrease the AAA by deductible losses and expenses, nondeductible expenses (other than expenses related to tax-exempt income)

notes.front: Can distributions reduce an S corporation’s AAA below zero?
notes.back: No. Distributions reduce the AAA, but not below zero.
notes.explanation: Distributions are taken into account after the year’s income and expenses, other than any net negative adjustment.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule M-2, Column (a). Accumulated Adjustments Account”, PDF p. 50
notes.evidence: Decrease AAA (but not below zero) by property distributions (other than dividend distributions from AE&P), unless the corporation elects to reduce AE&P first.

notes.front: Unless it elects otherwise, an S corporation’s distributions reduce the {{c1::AAA}} first, then previously taxed income, then accumulated earnings and profits.
notes.explanation: After those come the other adjustments account and any remaining shareholders’ equity accounts.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Distributions”, PDF p. 51
notes.evidence: Unless the corporation makes one of the elections described below, property distributions (including cash) are applied in the following order

notes.front: An S corporation that was once a C corporation has AAA of $10,000 and accumulated earnings and profits of $5,000, with no previously taxed income. It distributes $12,000 to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is large. How much is a dividend?
notes.choicesExplained: A treats the whole amount as coming from AAA. C treats the whole amount as coming from earnings and profits.
notes.explanation: $12,000 − $10,000 from AAA = $2,000 from accumulated earnings and profits, reported to the shareholder on Form 1099-DIV.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Line 17c. Dividend Distributions Paid From Accumulated Earnings and Profits”, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: Enter total dividends paid to shareholders from accumulated earnings and profits. Report these dividends to shareholders on Form 1099-DIV.

notes.front: Does tax-exempt income reported on Schedule K-1 increase a shareholder’s stock basis?
notes.back: Yes: basis rises by all income on Schedule K-1, including tax-exempt income.
notes.explanation: Unlike the AAA, which leaves tax-exempt income out, stock basis counts it.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Basis is increased by (a) all income (including tax-exempt income) reported on Schedule K-1

notes.front: A shareholder’s stock basis is reduced for distributions {{c1::before}} it is reduced for losses and deductions.
notes.explanation: The order is set out in the Schedule K-1 instructions: income, then distributions, then nondeductible expenses, then losses and deductions.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Basis is decreased (but not below zero) by (a) property distributions (including cash) made by the corporation reported in box 16, code D, of Schedule K-1

notes.front: Omar’s stock basis at 1 January 2025 is $10,000. His 2025 Schedule K-1 shows ordinary income $6,000, tax-exempt interest $1,000, nondeductible expenses $500 and a cash distribution of $12,000. What is his year-end stock basis?
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out the tax-exempt interest. C forgets the nondeductible expenses.
notes.explanation: Income of every kind goes in first, then the payout comes off, then the expenses: $10,000 + $6,000 + $1,000 = $17,000; − $12,000 = $5,000; − $500 = $4,500.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Basis is decreased (but not below zero) by (a) nondeductible expenses

notes.front: How is an S corporation distribution treated to the extent it exceeds the shareholder’s stock basis?
notes.back: As capital gain from the sale or exchange of property, reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D.
notes.explanation: Stock basis stops at zero; the excess is reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Box 16, Code D. Distributions”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: If these distributions exceed the basis of your stock, the excess is treated as capital gain from the sale or exchange of property and is reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D (Form 1040).

notes.front: After adding 2025 income, Priya’s stock basis in her S corporation (which has no earnings and profits) is $8,000. It then distributes $11,000 to her. What is the result?
notes.back: A: $3,000 capital gain and basis of $0.
notes.choices:
A) $3,000 capital gain; stock basis $0
B) $11,000 dividend; stock basis $8,000
C) No gain; stock basis −$3,000
notes.choicesExplained: B treats the distribution as a dividend, but there are no earnings and profits. C lets basis go below zero, which it cannot.
notes.explanation: $11,000 − $8,000 basis = $3,000 excess, taxed as capital gain; basis stops at zero.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Box 16, Code D. Distributions”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: If these distributions exceed the basis of your stock, the excess is treated as capital gain from the sale or exchange of property

notes.front: A shareholder has used up her stock basis but has $20,000 of loan basis. The S corporation distributes $5,000 to her. Which basis does the distribution reduce?
notes.back: B: neither; distributions don’t reduce loan basis.
notes.choices:
A) Loan basis, by $5,000
B) Neither: distributions don’t reduce loan basis
C) Both, half each
notes.choicesExplained: A and C apply distributions to loan basis, which the instructions rule out.
notes.explanation: With stock basis at zero, the $5,000 is treated as capital gain rather than cutting into the loan basis.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis of loans”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: When determining your basis in loans to the corporation, remember that: • Distributions don’t reduce loan basis

notes.front: A shareholder personally guarantees a $100,000 bank loan to his S corporation. He has made no payments under the guarantee. How much debt basis does the guarantee give him?
notes.choicesExplained: C and B give basis for a guarantee alone; basis comes only from payments he actually makes.
notes.explanation: A guaranteed or co-signed loan is not the shareholder’s loan to the corporation.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis of loans”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Loans that a shareholder guarantees or co-signs aren’t part of a shareholder’s loan basis. Shareholders only obtain basis from acting as a guarantee or in a similar capacity to the extent the shareholder makes a payment pursuant to the guarantee.

notes.front: What limits a shareholder’s deduction for their share of S corporation losses and deductions?
notes.back: The basis of their stock plus the basis of their loans to the corporation.
notes.explanation: Basis is the first of the loss limits, applied before the at-risk and passive activity limits.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Generally, the deduction for your share of aggregate losses and deductions reported on Schedule K-1 is limited to the basis of your stock and loans from you to the corporation.

notes.front: Which loss limitation does an S corporation shareholder apply first?
notes.back: The basis limitation, before the at-risk, passive activity and excess business loss limitations.
notes.explanation: Specific limits, such as those on a particular deduction, generally apply before the at-risk and passive loss limits.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Limitations on Losses, Deductions, and Credits”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: These limitations and the order in which you must apply them are as follows: the basis limitations, the at-risk limitations, the passive activity limitations, and the excess business loss limitations.

notes.front: What happens to an S corporation loss a shareholder cannot deduct because of the basis limit?
notes.back: It carries forward indefinitely and is deductible in a later year, subject to that year’s basis limit.
notes.explanation: Stock basis is generally figured at the end of the corporation’s tax year.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Any losses and deductions not allowed this year because of the basis limit can be carried forward indefinitely and deducted in a later year subject to the basis limit for that year.

notes.front: Ben’s share of his S corporation’s 2025 ordinary loss is $15,000. At year end, before the loss, his stock basis is $5,000 and his loan to the corporation has a basis of $7,000. How much loss can he deduct in 2025 under the basis limit?
notes.back: B: $12,000; $3,000 carries forward.
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores loan basis. C ignores the basis limit altogether.
notes.explanation: $5,000 stock + $7,000 loan = $12,000 allowed; $15,000 − $12,000 = $3,000 carried forward. Both bases fall to zero.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: the deduction for your share of aggregate losses and deductions reported on Schedule K-1 is limited to the basis of your stock and loans from you to the corporation.

notes.front: Which form does an S corporation shareholder generally use to figure stock and debt basis?
notes.back: Form 7203, S Corporation Shareholder Stock and Debt Basis Limitations.
notes.explanation: It follows the Schedule K-1 basis rules and is where the loss limit is worked out.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: You should generally use Form 7203

notes.front: A shareholder receives a Schedule K-1 showing a loss larger than her stock basis, and she has also lent money to the corporation. Which form should she generally use to work out how much of the loss her stock and debt basis allow?
notes.back: A: Form 7203.
notes.choices:
A) Form 7203
B) Form 6198
C) Form 1120-S
notes.choicesExplained: B is for the at-risk limit, which comes after the basis limit. C is the corporation’s own return.
notes.explanation: The basis limit is applied first, and Form 7203 figures aggregate stock and debt basis.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis Limitations”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: You should generally use Form 7203

notes.front: How are accident and health benefits for a 2% shareholder-employee treated by the S corporation?
notes.back: Included in wages subject to income tax withholding, but excludable from wages for social security and Medicare taxes.
notes.explanation: The 2% shareholder cannot be treated as an employee for the health benefit exclusion.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “Accident and Health Benefits: S corporation shareholders”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: you must include the value of accident or health benefits you provide to the employee in the employee's wages subject to federal income tax withholding. However, you can exclude the value of these benefits (other than payments for specific injuries or illnesses

notes.front: Where may a more-than-2% shareholder deduct health insurance paid by the S corporation for them?
notes.back: On Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 17, after it is reported in box 14 of their Form W-2.
notes.explanation: The corporation reports the premiums as an information item on the shareholder’s Form W-2.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Line 7. Compensation of Officers and Line 8. Salaries and Wages”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: as an information item in box 14 of that shareholder’s Form W-2. A more-than-2% shareholder may be allowed to deduct such amounts on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 17.

notes.front: Ana owned 3% of an S corporation until 31 March 2025, then sold down to 1% for the rest of the year. The corporation paid her health insurance all year. Is she a 2% shareholder for 2025?
notes.back: A: yes.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: she held more than 2% on some day of the year
B) No: she held 1% at year end
C) No: her average holding was under 2%
notes.choicesExplained: B looks only at year end and C averages the holding, but the rule asks whether she held more than 2% on any single day of the tax year.
notes.explanation: Ownership of more than 2% on any day of the tax year is enough.
notes.source: Publication 15-B (2025), Employer’s Tax Guide to Fringe Benefits, “Exception for S corporation shareholders”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: A 2% shareholder for this purpose is someone who directly or indirectly owns (for any day during the tax year) more than 2% of the corporation's stock

notes.front: When must distributions to an S corporation officer be treated as wages?
notes.back: To the extent they are reasonable compensation for services the officer rendered to the corporation.
notes.explanation: Calling pay for services a distribution does not change its character.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Line 7. Compensation of Officers and Line 8. Salaries and Wages”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Distributions and other payments by an S corporation to a corporate officer must be treated as wages to the extent the amounts are reasonable compensation for services rendered to the corporation.

notes.front: Sam, sole shareholder and full-time president of an S corporation, takes no salary but $90,000 of distributions for 2025. What is the likely issue?
notes.back: C: part must be treated as wages.
notes.choices:
A) None: distributions are never wages
B) All $90,000 is a dividend
C) Part of the $90,000 must be treated as wages, as reasonable pay for his services
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the reasonable compensation rule. B is wrong: nothing suggests earnings and profits.
notes.explanation: Payments to an officer are wages to the extent they are reasonable compensation for services he performs.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Line 7. Compensation of Officers and Line 8. Salaries and Wages”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: Distributions and other payments by an S corporation to a corporate officer must be treated as wages to the extent the amounts are reasonable compensation

notes.front: How is an S corporation’s net unrealised built-in gain measured?
notes.back: Aggregate fair market value of its assets at the start of its first S corporation year, minus their aggregate adjusted basis.
notes.explanation: The figure is then reduced by net recognised built-in gain from prior years.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule B, Item 8”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: The corporation’s net unrealized built-in gain is the amount, if any, by which the aggregate FMV of the assets of the corporation at the beginning of its first S corporation year

notes.front: A C corporation becomes an S corporation on 1 January 2025. On that day its assets are worth $900,000 in total and have an aggregate adjusted basis of $650,000. What is its net unrealised built-in gain?
notes.choicesExplained: A uses total value, ignoring basis. C uses the basis itself.
notes.explanation: $900,000 fair market value − $650,000 adjusted basis = $250,000.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Schedule B, Item 8”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: exceeds the aggregate adjusted basis of such assets at that time.

notes.front: When must an S corporation make estimated tax payments?
notes.back: When its built-in gains tax, excess net passive income tax and investment credit recapture tax total $500 or more.
notes.explanation: The required annual amount is generally the smaller of these taxes for the current year or a figure based partly on the prior year’s passive income tax.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Estimated Tax Payments”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: the corporation must make installment payments of estimated tax for the following taxes if the total of these taxes is $500 or more. (a) The tax on built-in gains. (b) The excess net passive income tax. (c) The investment credit recapture tax

notes.front: When does an S corporation owe the excess net passive income tax?
notes.back: When it has accumulated earnings and profits at year end and passive investment income above 25% of gross receipts.
notes.explanation: The instructions say it can apply where the corporation was previously a C corporation or took part in a tax-free reorganisation with one.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Line 23a. Excess Net Passive Income and LIFO Recapture Tax”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: If the corporation has AE&P at the close of its tax year and has passive investment income for the tax year that is in excess of 25% of gross receipts, the corporation must figure its excess net passive income and pay tax on it.

notes.front: What passive income test automatically ends an S election?
notes.back: Accumulated earnings and profits plus passive investment income over 25% of gross receipts, for 3 consecutive tax years.
notes.explanation: The corporation also pays tax on excess net passive income for each such year.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: For each of 3 consecutive tax years, the corporation (a) has accumulated earnings and profits (AE&P) and (b) derives more than 25% of its gross receipts from passive investment income

notes.front: A calendar-year S corporation with accumulated earnings and profits has passive investment income above 25% of gross receipts in 2023, 2024 and 2025. When does its election end?
notes.back: B: 1 January 2026.
notes.choices:
A) 31 December 2025
B) 1 January 2026
C) 1 January 2025
notes.choicesExplained: A ends it on the last day of the third year rather than the first day after. C ends it during the third year.
notes.explanation: The election ends on the first day of the first tax year beginning after the third consecutive year: 2023, 2024, 2025, then 1 January 2026.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: The election terminates on the first day of the first tax year beginning after the third consecutive tax year.

notes.front: What consent does revoking an S election need?
notes.back: Shareholders holding more than 50% of the issued and outstanding shares, counting nonvoting stock, when the revocation is made.
notes.explanation: The corporation files a statement signed by each consenting shareholder with the service center.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: An election can be revoked only with the consent of shareholders who, at the time the revocation is made, hold more than 50% of the number of issued and outstanding shares of stock (including nonvoting stock).

notes.front: Two shareholders sign a revocation: one holds voting shares equal to 30% of all issued shares, the other nonvoting shares equal to 25%. Is the revocation valid?
notes.back: A: yes, 55% consent.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 55% of the shares consent
B) No: only voting shares count
C) No: every shareholder must consent
notes.choicesExplained: B leaves out nonvoting stock, which counts. C applies the rule for making the election, not revoking it.
notes.explanation: 30% + 25% = 55% of issued and outstanding shares, which is more than 50%.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: hold more than 50% of the number of issued and outstanding shares of stock (including nonvoting stock).

notes.front: If a revocation names no effective date, when does it take effect?
notes.back: At the start of the tax year if made by the 15th day of its 3rd month; otherwise at the start of the next year.
notes.explanation: A revocation may instead name a date on or after the day it is filed.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If no date is specified, the revocation is effective at the start of the tax year if the revocation is made on or before the 15th day of the 3rd month of that tax year.

notes.front: A calendar-year S corporation files a valid revocation on 20 March 2026 with no effective date. When does it stop being an S corporation?
notes.back: A: 1 January 2027.
notes.choices:
A) 1 January 2027
B) 20 March 2026
C) 1 January 2026
notes.choicesExplained: C would need filing by 15 March. B would need that date to be specified.
notes.explanation: The 15th day of the 3rd month is 15 March; 20 March is later, so the revocation starts the next year.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: If no date is specified and the revocation is made after the 15th day of the 3rd month of the tax year, the revocation is effective at the start of the next tax year.

notes.front: When does an S election end if the corporation stops being a small business corporation?
notes.back: On the day it no longer meets the definition.
notes.explanation: The corporation attaches a statement to its final Form 1120-S giving notice of the termination and the date it occurred.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: This kind of termination of an election is effective as of the day the corporation no longer meets the definition of a small business corporation.

notes.front: On 1 July 2025 a calendar-year S corporation issues shares to a partnership. What is the effect?
notes.back: B: it ends on 1 July 2025.
notes.choices:
A) The election ends on 1 January 2026
B) The election ends on 1 July 2025
C) Nothing, until the Internal Revenue Service acts
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the passive income timing. C is wrong: termination is automatic.
notes.explanation: A partnership is not a permitted shareholder, so the corporation stops qualifying that day and the termination is immediate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: An election terminates automatically in any of the following cases. 1. The corporation is no longer a small business corporation as defined in section 1361(b).

notes.front: After an S election terminates, when may the corporation elect again without special consent?
notes.back: Not before the fifth tax year after the first tax year in which the termination took effect.
notes.explanation: Re-electing earlier needs the consent of the Internal Revenue Service.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: can make another election on Form 2553 only with IRS consent for any tax year before the fifth tax year after the first tax year in which the termination took effect.

notes.front: What can a corporation do if it believes its S election ended by an inadvertent termination?
notes.back: Ask the Internal Revenue Service for permission to continue to be treated as an S corporation.
notes.explanation: Relief applies to terminations from ceasing to qualify or from the passive income rule; Regulations section 1.1362-4 sets the requirements.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 1
notes.evidence: the corporation believes the termination was inadvertent, the Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025) corporation can ask for permission from the IRS to continue to be treated as an S corporation.

notes.front: When is Form 1120-S due for a calendar-year 2025 S corporation?
notes.back: 16 March 2026, because 15 March falls on a Sunday.
notes.explanation: The general rule is the 15th day of the 3rd month after the tax year ends, moved to the next business day.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: For calendar year corporations, the due date is March 16, 2026 (March 15th falls on Sunday).

notes.front: An S corporation has a fiscal year ending 30 June 2025. When is its Form 1120-S due, before extensions?
notes.back: A: 15 September 2025.
notes.choices:
A) 15 September 2025
B) 15 August 2025
C) 15 October 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B uses the 2nd month after year end. C uses the 4th month.
notes.explanation: Year ends 30 June; the 3rd month after is September, so the 15th of September (a Monday in 2025).
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “When To File”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Generally, an S corporation must file Form 1120-S by the 15 day of the 3rd month after the end of its tax year.

notes.front: What is the penalty for filing Form 1120-S late when no tax is due?
notes.back: $255 for each month or part of a month late, up to 12 months, times the number of shareholders.
notes.explanation: Every person who was a shareholder at any time during the year counts.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Late filing of return”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: For returns on which no tax is due, the penalty is $255 for each month or part of a month (up to 12 months) the return is late or doesn’t include the required information, multiplied by the total number of persons who were shareholders

notes.front: A calendar-year 2025 S corporation with 3 shareholders and no tax due files Form 1120-S on 10 July 2026, with no extension and no reasonable cause. What is the late filing penalty?
notes.choicesExplained: A forgets to multiply by the shareholders. C counts 5 months.
notes.explanation: Due 16 March 2026; 10 July is 3 full months plus part of a 4th late = 4 months. $255 × 4 months × 3 shareholders = $3,060.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Late filing of return”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: the penalty is $255 for each month or part of a month (up to 12 months) the return is late

notes.front: Where does an S corporation turn when its debt is discharged in a title 11 bankruptcy or while insolvent?
notes.back: Form 982, Reduction of Tax Attributes Due to Discharge of Indebtedness, and Pub. 908.
notes.explanation: The instructions point to these for the canceled debt exclusion.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Canceled debt exclusion”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: If the corporation has had debt discharged resulting from a title 11 bankruptcy proceeding or while insolvent, see Form 982, Reduction of Tax Attributes Due to Discharge of Indebtedness, and Pub. 908, Bankruptcy Tax Guide.

notes.front: How do distributions affect stock basis and loan basis differently?
notes.back: They reduce stock basis, with any excess taxed as capital gain, but they never reduce loan basis.
notes.explanation: Losses, by contrast, reduce stock basis first and then loan basis.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) (2025), “Basis of loans”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Distributions don’t reduce loan basis

notes.front: How does revoking an S election differ from its terminating?
notes.back: Revocation is chosen by shareholders holding more than 50%; termination happens automatically when a qualifying test fails.
notes.explanation: Both are listed together among the ways an election ends.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120-S (2025), “Termination of Election”, PDF p. 2
notes.evidence: Once the election is made, it stays in effect until it is terminated.
